topic: Solar system; stability of orbital motions; satellites (physics only)
subject: physics

items.q: Which statement correctly describes what our solar system contains?
items.correct: One star, eight planets, dwarf planets and their natural satellites
items.misconception: One star and eight planets only; dwarf planets are not included
items.why: Primary-school diagrams and models show only the Sun and eight planets in a neat row, so anything left out of that picture is not counted as belonging. The specification lists the members of the solar system as the Sun, the eight planets, the dwarf planets, and the natural satellites (moons) that orbit planets. All of them orbit within the Sun's gravitational field, so all of them belong.
items.random_wrong: One star, nine planets and the dwarf planets that orbit them

items.q: Which statement about the moons in our solar system is correct?
items.correct: They orbit planets, and they are part of the solar system
items.misconception: They orbit the Sun, keeping pace with the nearest planet
items.why: Students learn that the Sun's gravity dominates the solar system, and then apply that single idea to every body without asking which body each one actually circles. The defining feature of a natural satellite is that it orbits a planet: the Moon circles the Earth, held by the Earth's gravitational force. Planets and dwarf planets orbit the Sun; moons orbit planets.
items.random_wrong: They orbit planets, but they are not part of the solar system

items.q: How is our solar system related to the Milky Way galaxy?
items.correct: The solar system is a small part of the Milky Way galaxy
items.misconception: The Milky Way is one of the galaxies inside our solar system
items.why: The words 'solar system', 'galaxy' and 'universe' are all used loosely to mean 'space', so students never fix the order of scale between them. Fix the scale: one star (the Sun) with its planets makes our solar system; a huge number of stars makes the Milky Way galaxy; a huge number of galaxies makes the universe. The solar system sits inside the galaxy, not the other way round.
items.random_wrong: The solar system sits at the exact centre of the Milky Way

items.q: The Sun formed from a cloud of dust and gas called a nebula. What pulled this cloud together?
items.correct: The gravitational attraction between the parts of the cloud
items.misconception: The pressure wave from a nearby exploding star pushing it in
items.why: Students associate 'squashing something up' with pushing, and gravity is usually pictured as a downward pull on Earth rather than a mutual attraction between any masses. Every mass attracts every other mass. In a nebula this gravitational attraction pulls the dust and gas inwards, so the cloud contracts on its own. The specification names gravitational attraction as the cause.
items.random_wrong: The magnetic attraction between the dust grains in the cloud

items.q: As gravity draws the dust and gas of a nebula together, the material becomes denser and hotter. What does this eventually lead to?
items.correct: The temperature becomes high enough for fusion reactions to start
items.misconception: The gas begins to burn, releasing energy by chemical reaction
items.why: Everyday language ('burning', 'the Sun's fire') and the visible glow of flames make combustion the obvious model for anything hot and bright. Burning is a chemical reaction between substances and needs oxygen; it rearranges atoms but leaves nuclei untouched. Fusion is a nuclear change in which nuclei themselves join together, releasing far more energy.
items.random_wrong: The largest nuclei split apart, releasing energy by fission

items.q: Which nuclear process releases the energy of a newly formed star?
items.correct: Hydrogen nuclei fuse together to form helium nuclei
items.misconception: Large nuclei such as uranium split into smaller nuclei
items.why: Fission and fusion are met close together, both release energy and both begin with 'f', so the two processes get swapped. Fusion = fuse = join. Fission = split. In a star, hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium; that building-up process is also how heavier elements are made, which splitting could never do.
items.random_wrong: Hydrogen gas burns in oxygen to release heat and light

items.q: A main sequence star such as the Sun stays the same size for billions of years. Why?
items.correct: Gravity pulling it inwards is balanced by the expansion caused by fusion energy
items.misconception: Gravity no longer acts on the star once fusion reactions have started
items.why: Students read 'balanced' as 'one effect has been switched off', instead of two effects that are still there but equal and opposite. Both effects act at all times. Gravity keeps pulling the star inwards and the energy from fusion keeps pushing it outwards; because they are equal in size the star neither shrinks nor expands. If the fusion energy fell, gravity would immediately make the star contract.
items.random_wrong: The expansion caused by fusion is far stronger than the collapse

items.q: Suppose the energy released by fusion in a stable star suddenly fell. What would happen to the size of the star?
items.correct: It would contract, because gravity would then be unbalanced
items.misconception: It would expand, because gravity acts outwards from the centre
items.why: Students read 'balanced' as 'one effect has been switched off', instead of two effects that are still there but equal and opposite. Both effects act at all times. Gravity keeps pulling the star inwards and the energy from fusion keeps pushing it outwards; because they are equal in size the star neither shrinks nor expands. If the fusion energy fell, gravity would immediately make the star contract.
items.random_wrong: It would stay the same, because gravity stops once fusion starts

items.q: What determines the stages that a star passes through in its life cycle?
items.correct: The size of the star when it forms
items.misconception: The surface temperature of the star
items.why: Colour and temperature are the properties students can most easily observe or picture, so they are assumed to be the controlling factor. The specification is explicit: the life cycle is determined by the size of the star. Two stars of very different sizes follow different routes after the main sequence, however hot or old either of them is.
items.random_wrong: The colour the star appears from Earth

items.q: A star the size of the Sun comes to the end of its main sequence stage. Which sequence of stages follows?
items.correct: Red giant, then white dwarf, then black dwarf
items.misconception: White dwarf, then red giant, then black dwarf
items.why: Students assume a star must get steadily smaller as it dies, so the biggest stage cannot come after the smallest. Learn the sequence in order: nebula, protostar, main sequence, red giant, white dwarf, black dwarf. The star expands into a red giant when its main sequence stage ends, then sheds its outer layers to leave the hot, dense white dwarf.
items.random_wrong: Red giant, then supernova, then neutron star

items.q: The Sun will eventually run out of hydrogen in its core. What will it finally become?
items.correct: A white dwarf, which then cools to form a black dwarf
items.misconception: A black hole, formed when its core collapses inwards
items.why: Supernovae and black holes dominate films and documentaries, so they become the default ending for any star. Only stars much more massive than the Sun end in a supernova and leave a neutron star or a black hole. A star the size of the Sun becomes a red giant, then a white dwarf, then a black dwarf.
items.random_wrong: A supernova, which throws its outer layers outwards

items.q: A star much more massive than the Sun leaves the main sequence. Which sequence of stages follows?
items.correct: Red super giant, then supernova, then neutron star or black hole
items.misconception: Red giant, then white dwarf, then black dwarf as the star cools
items.why: Supernovae and black holes dominate films and documentaries, so they become the default ending for any star. Only stars much more massive than the Sun end in a supernova and leave a neutron star or a black hole. A star the size of the Sun becomes a red giant, then a white dwarf, then a black dwarf.
items.random_wrong: Red super giant, then supernova, then a black hole in every case

items.q: After a supernova, what decides whether the remnant left behind is a neutron star or a black hole?
items.correct: The mass of the star that exploded
items.misconception: The colour of the supernova flash
items.why: Colour and temperature are the properties students can most easily observe or picture, so they are assumed to be the controlling factor. The specification is explicit: the life cycle is determined by the size of the star. Two stars of very different sizes follow different routes after the main sequence, however hot or old either of them is.
items.random_wrong: The surface temperature of the star

items.q: Where are the naturally occurring elements heavier than iron produced?
items.correct: In a supernova, the explosion of a massive star
items.misconception: In the main sequence stage of any large star
items.why: Students learn correctly that fusion in stars produces the naturally occurring elements, and then apply it without noticing the limit the specification places on it. Fusion in stars builds nuclei up as far as iron. Elements heavier than iron are produced in a supernova, so a star that never explodes never makes them.
items.random_wrong: In the core of every star, along with iron

items.q: How do fusion processes inside a star lead to the formation of new elements?
items.correct: Nuclei join to make heavier nuclei, building elements up to iron
items.misconception: Heavy nuclei split, so lighter elements build up in the core
items.why: Fission and fusion are met close together, both release energy and both begin with 'f', so the two processes get swapped. Fusion = fuse = join. Fission = split. In a star, hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium; that building-up process is also how heavier elements are made, which splitting could never do.
items.random_wrong: Nuclei join, producing every element up to uranium in the core

items.q: The Earth contains elements such as gold and lead. How did these elements come to be in the material from which the Earth formed?
items.correct: A supernova explosion spread them out across the universe
items.misconception: They were formed inside the Earth after it had cooled
items.why: Students meet elements first in chemistry as fixed, given substances, so nothing prompts them to ask where the atoms themselves came from. Fusion processes in stars produce all the naturally occurring elements, and the explosion of a massive star distributes those elements throughout the universe. The material the Earth formed from already contained them.
items.random_wrong: They were made by fusion inside the Sun and blown out

items.q: A satellite moves in a circular orbit around the Earth. What keeps it in that orbit?
items.correct: The gravitational force of the Earth acting on the satellite
items.misconception: Nothing does; there is no force acting on it out in space
items.why: Footage of astronauts floating is read as proof that gravity has vanished, and 'zero gravity' is used as an everyday label for it. The Earth's gravitational field extends far into space; without it a satellite would travel in a straight line and leave. It is the gravitational force that continually pulls the satellite towards the Earth and so keeps it in orbit.
items.random_wrong: Balanced forces: gravity inwards and a force outwards

items.q: What do the Moon and a communications satellite orbiting the Earth have in common?
items.correct: Both are kept in orbit by gravity
items.misconception: Both were launched into orbit by people
items.why: Everyday use of the word 'satellite' (satellite TV, satellite dish) refers only to technology, so the natural meaning is never met. Natural and artificial satellites are alike in that both orbit a planet and both are held in orbit by gravity. The distinction is only in origin: moons formed naturally, artificial satellites were built and launched by people.
items.random_wrong: Both travel in orbit around the Sun

items.q: A satellite travels round a circular orbit at a steady speed. Which statement about its motion is correct?
items.correct: Its velocity changes because its direction keeps changing
items.misconception: Its velocity is constant because its speed is constant
items.why: Speed and velocity are used as synonyms in ordinary speech, so the vector nature of velocity is easily forgotten once numbers are involved. Velocity is speed in a given direction, so a change of direction alone is a change of velocity. In a circular orbit gravity acts at right angles to the motion, turning the satellite without speeding it up.
items.random_wrong: Its speed increases because gravity is always pulling on it

items.q: A satellite in a stable circular orbit is made to travel at a greater speed. What must happen if the orbit is to stay stable?
items.correct: The radius of its orbit must decrease
items.misconception: The radius of its orbit can stay the same
items.why: The everyday picture is a car going faster round the same roundabout, where the driver simply steers harder; students do not notice that a satellite cannot choose its inward force. The gravitational force at a given distance is fixed, and only one speed matches that force. Change the speed and the orbit is no longer stable at that distance: for a stable orbit at a higher speed the radius must be smaller.
items.random_wrong: The radius of its orbit must increase

items.q: What kind of object is the Sun?
items.correct: The Sun is a star, and it is the only star in our solar system.
items.misconception: The Sun is not really a star; it is a huge ball of fire at the centre, and the stars are the small points of light you see at night.
items.why: The Sun looks nothing like a night-time star because it is so much closer, and everyday language treats 'sun' and 'star' as different words for different things. A star is a body that releases energy by nuclear fusion and emits its own light; the Sun does exactly that. The other stars look like faint points only because they are enormously further away.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How many planets orbit the Sun?
items.correct: Eight.
items.misconception: There are nine planets, because Pluto is one of them.
items.why: Older books, posters and family memory still list nine planets, and Pluto is often the most memorable name on the list. The specification states that the solar system contains eight planets. Pluto is classed as a dwarf planet: it still orbits the Sun and is still part of the solar system, but it is not one of the eight planets.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Where is the Sun within the Milky Way galaxy?
items.correct: The Sun is one ordinary star among the enormous number in the galaxy, and the solar system is only a small part of it.
items.misconception: The Sun must sit at the centre of the Milky Way, because everything orbits the Sun.
items.why: Students correctly learn that the Sun is at the centre of the solar system and then stretch that fact to the whole galaxy. The Sun is at the centre of our solar system only. On the scale of the galaxy it is one star among a vast number, and the specification stresses that our solar system is a small part of the Milky Way.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which comes first, the gravitational collapse of the cloud or the fusion reactions?
items.correct: Gravity draws the dust and gas together first; the resulting rise in temperature then causes fusion reactions to begin.
items.misconception: The fusion energy is what draws the cloud together, so the star is already fusing before it collapses.
items.why: Fusion is the most striking idea in the topic, so students make it the cause of everything rather than a consequence of the collapse. Follow the order in the specification: dust and gas drawn together by gravity causes fusion reactions. The contraction raises the temperature and density enough for nuclei to fuse; fusion is the result, not the trigger.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: When do fusion reactions start in a forming star?
items.correct: Only once gravity has made the protostar dense and hot enough for hydrogen nuclei to fuse.
items.misconception: Fusion starts as soon as the dust and gas begin to gather, so any clump of gas in space is a star.
items.why: Students see 'gas cloud' and 'star' on the same diagram and treat the change as instant, with no condition attached. Fusion needs extremely high temperature and density. Gravity supplies these by compressing the material of the protostar; until that threshold is reached there is no fusion, and the object is not yet a star.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do all stars end their lives in a supernova?
items.correct: No. Only stars much more massive than the Sun explode as a supernova.
items.misconception: Every star finishes with a supernova; it is just the normal way a star dies.
items.why: The supernova is the memorable event in the topic, and students who learn only one ending apply it to every star. The route a star takes is determined by its size. A star the size of the Sun ends quietly as a white dwarf and then a black dwarf; there is no explosion. A supernova belongs only to the massive route.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What is left behind after a supernova?
items.correct: A neutron star, or a black hole if the original star was massive enough.
items.misconception: Every supernova leaves a black hole, and a neutron star is just another name for one.
items.why: Both remnants are described as extremely dense, and students who meet them together compress two outcomes into one. There are two possible outcomes, and which one occurs depends on the mass of the original star. Massive stars leave a neutron star; the most massive of all leave a black hole, from which not even light can escape.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are the forces on an orbiting satellite balanced?
items.correct: No. There is a resultant gravitational force on the satellite, directed towards the Earth.
items.misconception: The satellite stays in orbit because gravity pulling inwards is balanced by an outward force that throws it out.
items.why: Students expect steady motion to mean balanced forces, and the feeling of being flung outwards on a fairground ride supplies an invented outward force. Nothing pushes the satellite outwards. The single unbalanced gravitational force acts towards the centre of the orbit and continually changes the satellite's direction; that is precisely what keeps it circling instead of flying off in a straight line.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Gravity pulls on an orbiting satellite. Why does the satellite not get faster and faster?
items.correct: Because in a circular orbit the gravitational force acts at right angles to the direction of motion, so it changes the direction of travel but not the speed.
items.misconception: A force always makes something speed up, so gravity must be making the satellite go faster all the time.
items.why: Every earlier example of a force acting on a moving object - a falling ball, a car accelerating - has the force along the direction of motion, so students expect the same here. What a force does depends on its direction relative to the motion. A force along the motion changes speed; a force at right angles to it changes only direction. Gravity on a circular orbit is always at right angles to the motion, pointing to the centre.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can a satellite orbit stably at any radius with any speed?
items.correct: No. For each radius there is one speed that gives a stable orbit, so speed and radius are linked.
items.misconception: Any combination will do; a satellite orbits wherever it is put, at whatever speed it happens to have.
items.why: Diagrams show satellites at several different heights without stating the speed, leaving the impression that the two quantities are independent. Speed and radius are tied together for a stable orbit: satellites in low orbits must travel faster than those in high orbits. If the speed is wrong for the radius, the orbit is not stable and the radius changes.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
